newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian sorghum still finds support - Grainco.
newsitem.headline: Australian sorghum still finds support - Grainco.

text.p: Domestic Australian sorghum values in southern Queensland continued to be supported by lack of grower selling, dry weather and to some extent a steady export market, Queensland grain co-operative Grainco Ltd said.
Growers were reluctant sellers of sorghum as they waited for rain to begin winter planting, trading manager Rob Brealey said in Grainco's weekly market report.
Central Queensland also wanted rain, particularly in the northern highlands, for summer crops and the winter planting, he said.
In central Queensland, values finished the week around A$131.00 a tonne delivered port, again reflecting the volatility in the export market over the past week, Brealey said.
Domestic Australian feed barley values continued well supported with growers reluctant to commit the balance of their grain while dry weather persisted in southern Queensland.
Domestic demand remained relatively subdued with some business transacted over the past week from northern New South Wales (NSW). Tonnage appeared minor.
Prices finished around A$160 a tonne Queensland origin.
Values continued to track the export market, which remained volatile as the U.S. attempted to shed its winter coat and enter the corn planting window, he said.

Both domestic and export sorghum markets watched the international wheat market very closely as concern emerged about crop losses from late winter kill in some northern states of the U.S. together with concern about dry conditions in Europe.
The nearby sorghum market continued steady, with values trading late last week at around A$150 a tonne delivered Brisbane, while May and June paid a premium over April.

New crop export values received some support over the past week from reports of dry weather in parts of Europe, particularly Spain and France, and continuing dry conditions in Victoria and South Australia.
With expectations of a smaller barley planting in North America this year, problems with Europe or Australia would support values longer-term, he said.
The international malting barley market remained quiet with most buyers covered in the short-term. The next round of Chinese buying would begin in June for August/September shipment.
The market will now look to European and Canadian crop prospects and the planting fortunes of the Australian crop in May/June for direction, he said.
Trade was light in cottonseed in Queensland in recent weeks.
Domestic business has picked up with dry weather persisting. As well as increased dairy usage there has been an increase in supplementary feeding for grazing stock.
Export markets have shown further interest in additional coverage. But with the domestic market kicking, export consumers prices are lagging behind domestic values.
While consumers in the north Asian region still require substantial cottonseed coverage, the firmer Australian price is driving them to look for cheaper alternate supplies.

Prices should remain firm at around the current level of A$140 a tonne ex-gin, particularly if the dry spell continues. Cottonseed at this level is seen as reasonable value by the domestic feed market.
However, a weather break would allow favourable conditions for winter crop plantings, which may ease price pressure.
Domestic oilseed values rose over the past week, with sunflowers finishing at A$320 a tonne Brisbane for April 1997.
Central Queensland new crop black sunflower prices were around A$260-A$265 a tonne depot for May-July 1997.
New crop soybean prices traded lower at A$412 Brisbane.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
